title: Infinite things — overview and the honesty rule
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. This database catalogs things that are genuinely infinite — not merely huge, but without end by proof or by the structure of mathematics. The honesty rule governs every record: "infinite" is claimed only where mathematics proves it or the definition entails it. Everything else — the merely vast, the effectively inexhaustible, the not-yet-measured — is labeled exactly as such.

The distinction matters because "infinite" is the most abused word in popular science. The number of possible chess games is about 10^120 — the Shannon number, a real published estimate — which is finite, however mind-bending. The digits of pi, by contrast, truly never end, because pi is irrational and that is proven. One is vast; the other is infinite. The database never confuses them.

Each record states the kind of infinity involved where mathematics provides kinds: countable infinities like the integers, uncountable ones like the real numbers. And each record carries its proof sketch or its definitional argument, so the claim can be checked rather than taken on faith.
capabilities: Claim infinite only where proof or definition entails it
Label the merely vast as vast, never as infinite
Distinguish countable from uncountable infinity
Carry a proof sketch or definitional argument per record
Correct the popular confusions explicitly

title: The primes are infinite — Euclid's proof
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. There are infinitely many prime numbers, and the proof is over two thousand years old. Euclid's argument, from the Elements (circa 300 BCE): suppose you have a finite list of all primes. Multiply them all together and add one. The result is either prime itself or has a prime factor — and that prime factor cannot be any prime on your list, because each one leaves remainder one. Contradiction. So no finite list contains all primes.

The proof is constructive in spirit: given any finite set of primes, it manufactures a new one outside the set. Run it on {2,3,5,7,11,13} and you get 30031, which is 59 times 509 — both new primes. The machine never stops producing.

This record is the database's gold standard for an infinity claim: ancient, short, checkable by hand, and load-bearing — modern cryptography's RSA system depends on the endless supply of large primes this proof guarantees.
capabilities: State Euclid's proof from the Elements, circa 300 BCE
Demonstrate the construction on {2,3,5,7,11,13}
Show the proof manufactures a new prime from any finite list
Note the modern load: RSA needs the endless prime supply
Hold this as the gold standard for infinity claims

title: The digits of pi never end — irrationality
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. Pi's decimal expansion never terminates and never settles into a repeating pattern, because pi is an irrational number — proven by Johann Heinrich Lambert in 1761. An irrational number cannot be written as a fraction of integers, and any terminating or repeating decimal can be, so pi's digits go on forever without repetition.

Computers have calculated trillions of pi's digits, and every digit computed is just a waypoint on an endless road. The normality question — whether every digit appears equally often — remains open; the database reports that honestly rather than claiming it. What is proven is infinitude of digits, and that is enough for this record.

The philosophical footnote the record keeps: pi's infinite digits are all "already there" in the number itself. Nobody is generating them; computation only reveals them. It is the purest infinite thing in the database — no process, no growth, just an endless fact.
capabilities: State Lambert 1761: pi is irrational, digits never repeat-end
Distinguish proven infinitude from open normality
Report trillions of computed digits as waypoints, not progress
Note the digits are revealed, not generated
Keep the philosophical footnote clearly marked

title: The natural numbers — no largest number
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. The natural numbers 1, 2, 3, ... have no largest member. Proof: for any natural number n, n+1 is a natural number larger than n. Two lines, no assumptions beyond the definition. This is the simplest infinity in mathematics and the foundation every other infinity in this database stands on.

Children discover it independently — "a million!" "a million and one!" — and the database honors that: the intuition is correct and the proof is its formal clothing. The Peano axioms, published by Giuseppe Peano in 1889, formalize the successor operation that makes the argument airtight.

The record also guards the boundary: the natural numbers are infinite, but any particular natural number is finite. Infinity is a property of the set, not of its members. Confusing the two is the most common error in casual talk about infinity, and this database does not make it.
capabilities: Prove no largest natural number via the successor step
Cite Peano 1889 for the formal successor axioms
Honor the childhood intuition as genuinely correct
Guard the boundary: the set is infinite, members are finite
Use this as the foundation for all other infinity records

title: Fractals — infinite detail in finite space
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. The Mandelbrot set — defined by the simple iteration z = z^2 + c over complex numbers, studied by Benoit Mandelbrot in 1980 — contains infinite detail inside a finite region of the plane. Zoom into its boundary at any magnification and new structure appears: spirals, seahorses, filaments, each resolving into more structure on closer zoom, without end.

This is infinity of a different flavor from the primes: not endless counting but endless resolution. The set's boundary has infinite length packed into finite area, a fact that follows from its self-similar structure at all scales. The definition is finite — one short equation — and the detail it generates is not.

The database notes the physical caveat honestly: real-world "fractals" like coastlines and snowflakes stop being fractal at atomic scales. Mathematical fractals do not stop. The record claims infinity only for the mathematics, exactly as the honesty rule requires.
capabilities: Define the Mandelbrot set via z = z^2 + c, Mandelbrot 1980
Describe endless boundary structure at every magnification
Distinguish infinite resolution from infinite extent
Note real-world fractals stop at atomic scales
Claim infinity for the mathematics only

title: Hilbert's hotel — the countable infinity paradox
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. Hilbert's hotel is a thought experiment from mathematician David Hilbert's lectures, popularized by George Gamow in 1947: a hotel with infinitely many rooms, all occupied, can still take new guests. Move each guest from room n to room n+1 and room 1 opens up. For infinitely many new guests, move each guest from room n to room 2n and all odd rooms open up.

The hotel is not a place; it is a demonstration that infinite sets behave unlike finite ones. "Full" does not mean "no room" when the rooms are countably infinite. The arithmetic is exact and the database's demo program performs the room shifts.

The record is careful about what the hotel proves: it proves things about the mathematics of infinite sets, not about real hotels. No physical hotel has infinitely many rooms. The infinity lives in the structure of the natural numbers, and the hotel is just its most memorable costume.
capabilities: Tell the hotel story per Hilbert via Gamow 1947
Perform the n to n+1 shift for finitely many new guests
Perform the n to 2n shift for infinitely many new guests
State what is proven: facts about infinite sets
Deny the physical reading: no real hotel is infinite

title: Zeno and calculus — infinite steps that finish
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. Zeno of Elea's paradoxes, from around 450 BCE, argued that motion is impossible because any journey requires infinitely many half-steps: half the distance, then half the remainder, then half of that, forever. The resolution took two millennia: the infinite series 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... sums to exactly 1. Infinitely many steps, finite total.

Calculus, developed by Newton and Leibniz in the 17th century, made this rigorous with limits: the partial sums approach 1 as closely as desired. The infinite process completes because the steps shrink fast enough. Not all infinite series converge — 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... (the harmonic series) diverges to infinity, proven by Nicole Oresme in the 14th century — and the database records both cases.

The lesson the record draws: infinity is not a single behavior. Some infinities sum to one, some diverge without bound, and telling them apart is the whole subject of analysis. The database respects that variety.
capabilities: Tell Zeno's dichotomy paradox, circa 450 BCE
Sum 1/2 + 1/4 + ... to exactly 1 via limits
Contrast with the divergent harmonic series, Oresme 14th century
Credit Newton and Leibniz for rigorous limits
Draw the lesson: infinities have different behaviors

title: The Shannon number — vast but finite (the honesty exhibit)
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. The Shannon number — about 10^120 possible chess games — is the database's honesty exhibit: a quantity so large it feels infinite, and is not. Claude Shannon published the estimate in 1950, and it remains the standard illustration of combinatorial vastness. The number of possible Go games is even larger, around 10^170 by some estimates. Both are finite.

The record exists to calibrate the reader. A chess game tree that no computer will ever fully explore is still a finite tree. "Effectively inexhaustible" is a true and useful description; "infinite" would be false. The database uses the exact phrase "effectively inexhaustible" for such quantities and reserves "infinite" for the proven cases.

The trawler lesson: vast search spaces are where mix-and-match thrives — the combinations of mechanisms and problems are Shannon-like in their plenty. But the trawler never calls its well infinite. Bottomless in practice, finite in principle, honest in the record.
capabilities: State the Shannon number ~10^120, Shannon 1950
Note Go game estimates ~10^170, also finite
Use "effectively inexhaustible" for the merely vast
Reserve "infinite" for proven cases only
Calibrate the trawler's combination well as vast, not infinite

title: Countable vs uncountable — Cantor's two infinities
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. Georg Cantor proved in the 1870s–1890s that not all infinities are the same size. The natural numbers are countably infinite — they can be listed. The real numbers are uncountably infinite: Cantor's diagonal argument shows that any attempted list of reals misses at least one. There are strictly more real numbers than natural numbers, though both sets are infinite.

The diagonal argument is short enough to belong in this record: list binary decimals, flip the nth digit of the nth entry, and the result differs from every entry on the list. No complete list exists. The database's demo performs the diagonal on a finite list to show the mechanism.

This is the deepest record in the database: infinity comes in sizes, and the sizes themselves go on without end — Cantor showed there is no largest infinity either. The record states this carefully, because it is the closest mathematics comes to the database's title subject.
capabilities: State Cantor's result: reals outnumber naturals, 1870s-1890s
Walk through the diagonal argument step by step
Demonstrate the diagonal mechanism on a finite list
Note there is no largest infinity either
Mark this as the database's deepest record

title: Infinite tilings — covering the plane forever
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. A tiling that covers the infinite plane with no gaps is an infinite thing by definition: the pattern never ends because the plane never ends. The square grid is the simplest; the Penrose tilings, discovered by Roger Penrose in the 1970s, are the most remarkable — aperiodic tilings made of just two tile shapes that cover the plane forever without ever repeating.

The 2023 discovery of the "hat" monotile — a single shape that tiles the plane only aperiodically, by David Smith and collaborators — extended the story: even one tile suffices for endless non-repeating coverage. The database reports this as recent, real mathematics.

The record's quiet point: infinity here is definitional. The plane is unbounded, so any full tiling of it is unbounded too. No paradox, no trick — just the straightforward consequence of covering an endless surface with finite pieces.
capabilities: Define infinite tilings via the unbounded plane
Describe Penrose aperiodic tilings, 1970s, two tiles
Report the 2023 hat monotile discovery accurately
Note the infinity is definitional, not paradoxical
Keep the tone straightforward: endless surface, endless tiles

title: Convergent series — infinity that equals a number
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked. Some infinite sums equal ordinary finite numbers, and the record collects the cleanest examples. 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + ... = 1. 1/4 + 1/16 + 1/64 + ... = 1/3. The Basel problem's answer — 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + ... = pi^2/6 — was found by Euler in 1734 and stunned his contemporaries: the squares' reciprocals sum to pi squared over six.

Each equality is a small miracle of analysis: infinitely many terms, each smaller than the last, accumulating to exactly a finite value. The proofs use limits, and the database sketches the geometric-series argument rather than hand-waving.

The record closes the public edition by returning to the theme: infinity is not one thing. Sometimes it counts without end, sometimes it resolves without end, sometimes it sums to one. The database catalogs the varieties without pretending they are the same.
capabilities: Sum the geometric series 1/2 + 1/4 + ... = 1
State Euler 1734: Basel sum equals pi^2/6
Sketch the limit argument, never hand-wave
Collect convergent examples as a family
Close on the theme: infinity has varieties

title: Is the universe infinite — the open question
body:
Public edition. Public reference knowledge, fact-checked, with uncertainty labeled. Current cosmological measurements are consistent with a spatially flat universe, and a flat universe in the standard model is spatially infinite — but the measurements have error bars, and a universe much larger than the observable part would look flat too. The honest statement: the universe may be infinite; it is not established.

The observable universe is finite and measured: about 93 billion light-years across. Beyond that edge we cannot see, by the physics of light travel time, not by any wall. What lies beyond is constrained by theory and unmeasured in fact, and the database refuses to fill the gap with assertion.

This record is the public edition's integrity capstone. A database about infinity that claimed the universe is infinite without proof would betray its own honesty rule. So it says what is known, marks what is open, and lets the question stand — infinite or not, the universe has not finished answering.
capabilities: Report flat-universe measurements with their error bars
State the observable universe: ~93 billion light-years, finite
Explain why beyond is unobservable: light travel time
Refuse to assert what is not established
Let the open question stand as the integrity capstone
